questions.prompt: A cache-aside write invalidates the cache before updating the database. Which race can occur?

choices.text: Every reader is automatically blocked until the write completes.
Invalidation atomically commits both cache and database changes.
The cache changes into write-through mode for that request.
A reader can repopulate the cache with the old database value.

questions.explanation: A read between invalidation and the store update can cache old data. The two operations are not atomic, and invalidation does not change the caching pattern.

sources.title: Cache-Aside pattern
sources.claim: Cache-aside loads misses from the store, fills the cache, and writes the store before invalidating cached data.

questions.prompt: Two API instances cache one record locally. A write invalidates only one instance. What should the design account for?

choices.text: Cache expiry makes every read immediately strongly consistent.
Independent local caches necessarily share one memory entry.
The other instance can retain a stale local copy.
A local invalidation always broadcasts to every instance.

questions.explanation: Private caches can diverge. A distributed mechanism or explicit expiry/invalidation strategy is needed; expiry bounds retention rather than creating immediate consistency.

sources.title: Cache-Aside pattern
sources.claim: Cache-aside does not guarantee consistency, and local caches can diverge; expiry must balance staleness and repeated loading.

questions.prompt: A response has Cache-Control: no-cache. What does that directive mean in its unqualified form?

choices.text: Cache only the body and discard every response header.
Validate with the origin before reusing the response.
Never store the response in any cache under any circumstances.
Reuse it indefinitely without contacting the origin.

questions.explanation: no-cache controls reuse through validation. It is not the same as no-store and does not permit unvalidated indefinite reuse.

sources.title: RFC 9111: HTTP Caching
sources.claim: Unqualified no-cache requires successful validation before reuse; freshness and validation are distinct mechanisms.

questions.prompt: A personalized response uses Cache-Control: private. Which cache may store it subject to other rules?

choices.text: A private browser cache.
Any shared proxy cache because private means encrypted.
Every CDN cache as long as the response has a cookie.
No cache because private is identical to no-store.

questions.explanation: Unqualified private prohibits shared-cache storage while permitting private caches. It does not encrypt content or mean no-store.

sources.title: RFC 9111: HTTP Caching
sources.claim: Unqualified private prohibits shared-cache storage but permits private storage; no-store applies to both private and shared caches.

questions.prompt: A record is absent from a cache-aside cache. Which sequence is appropriate?

choices.text: Return permanent failure because cache misses cannot be loaded.
Write an empty record to the database before checking it.
Invalidate every other key and assume the missing value appears.
Read the store, cache the value, then return it.

questions.explanation: Cache-aside loads the requested value from its underlying store. The cache is an optimization, not the only source of the record.

sources.title: Cache-Aside pattern
sources.claim: Cache-aside reads misses from the source and then fills the cache.

questions.prompt: Reducing a local cache TTL improves freshness but sharply increases database reads. Which tradeoff is visible?

choices.text: A shorter TTL guarantees that no stale read can ever occur.
More database reads prove that caching no longer has any valid use.
More frequent refresh reduces retention but increases loading cost.
Expiry changes every cache lookup into a database transaction lock.

questions.explanation: Shorter retention can reduce stale duration while increasing misses. It does not guarantee immediate consistency or make caching categorically useless.

sources.title: Cache-Aside pattern
sources.claim: Cache-aside local copies can diverge and expiry trades freshness against repeated store access.

questions.prompt: Which operations fit cache-aside? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Assume every external database change immediately updates the cache.
Treat cache-aside as identical to updating both stores in the write path.
Read the data store and populate the cache on a miss.
Update the store before invalidating its cached item.
Use invalidation as an atomic transaction with every database write.

questions.explanation: A is incorrect: External changes can leave stale cached values. B is incorrect: That describes write-through behavior rather than invalidation on write. C is correct: Cache-aside loads data on demand. D is correct: This order reduces repopulation with pre-update data. E is incorrect: The ordinary pattern does not make both stores atomic.

sources.title: Cache-Aside pattern
sources.claim: Cache-aside loads misses from the store, fills the cache, and writes the store before invalidating cached data.

questions.prompt: Which cache-expiry tradeoffs matter? Select all that apply.

choices.text: A cache hit proves the value is the latest authoritative data.
Very short expiry can cause repeated loads from the data store.
Very long expiry can preserve stale values for too long.
Private instance caches can diverge after independent updates.
An expiry policy guarantees immediate freshness after every external write.

questions.explanation: A is incorrect: A hit can contain older data. B is correct: Premature expiration reduces cache benefits. C is correct: Retention affects data freshness. D is correct: Each instance can hold its own copy. E is incorrect: The value may remain stale until it is refreshed.

sources.title: Cache-Aside pattern
sources.claim: Cache-aside does not guarantee consistency, and local caches can diverge; expiry must balance staleness and repeated loading.

questions.prompt: Which HTTP cache-validation claims follow RFC 9111? Select all that apply.

choices.text: An unqualified no-cache response needs successful validation before reuse.
Freshness lifetime and validation serve different cache decisions.
no-cache and no-store always have identical storage semantics.
A stale response is always reusable even when must-revalidate applies.
A stored response with no-cache can be served without origin validation.

questions.explanation: A is correct: The directive requires contacting the origin for validation. B is correct: A fresh response can be reused while validation checks a stored response. C is incorrect: no-cache can allow storage but restricts reuse. D is incorrect: Explicit revalidation restrictions prohibit that reuse. E is incorrect: That contradicts the unqualified directive.

sources.title: RFC 9111: HTTP Caching
sources.claim: Unqualified no-cache requires successful validation before reuse; freshness and validation are distinct mechanisms.

questions.prompt: Which cache-control distinctions hold? Select all that apply.

choices.text: no-store ordinarily prohibits intentional storage in private and shared caches.
s-maxage applies its age limit to shared caches.
private encrypts the response content against interception.
public makes a personalized response safe for every user automatically.
Unqualified private forbids a shared cache from storing the response.

questions.explanation: A is correct: It applies across both cache types. B is correct: It overrides max-age or Expires for shared caches. C is incorrect: It controls storage location rather than transport confidentiality. D is incorrect: Caching permission does not establish correct user isolation. E is correct: The response is intended for a single user.

sources.title: RFC 9111: HTTP Caching
sources.claim: Unqualified private prohibits shared-cache storage but permits private storage; no-store applies to both private and shared caches.
